title: Tamagotchi
lede: Bandai’s egg-shaped virtual pet, sold as “the tiny pet from cyberspace”, made a pocket blobject out of a digital toy.
summary: Pink egg-shaped plastic toy with a small LCD and bead chain, on a blister card. Bandai, 1996–1997.

creator.name: Aki Maita and Akihiro Yokoi, for Bandai

made: 1997 (V&A copy); first released in Japan on 23 November 1996 per Wikipedia

evidence.note: Inspected the V&A photograph of object B.239-1997 (image 2006AE9151, 1200 × 1600), which shows the toy in its blister pack, in a scratchpad copy. Not stored.

styles.note: Partial fit: an egg-shaped blobject in candy pink and lime with a clear plastic bubble, marketed as coming from cyberspace. The card art is hand-drawn, not techno.
Partial fit: a candy-pink egg toy with hand-drawn card art of a cute digital pet, but the photographed object shows no character face.

context: The V&A calls it “one of the biggest toy fads of the late-1990s” and describes an egg-shaped virtual pet “made from pink and green plastic” with an LCD screen and a metal chain, sealed in a clear bubble pack printed in five languages. [V&A B.239-1997](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O37315/tamagotchi-video-game-yokoi-akihiro/).

Wikipedia gives the Japanese release as 23 November 1996 and the United States release as 1 May 1997, and says nearly 40 million units had sold by spring 1998. [Wikipedia: Tamagotchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamagotchi).
observed: The toy is a hot-pink egg with a lime-green face ring printed with numbers and a small square LCD in the center.
A silver bead chain loops from its top.
The blister pack is a clear plastic bubble with ribbed, rounded edges on a white card.
The card shows the Tamagotchi name in hand-drawn magenta capitals and three loose crayon-style drawings of an egg hatching; the slogan reads “The tiny pet from cyberspace”.
interpretation: The object, not the packaging, carries the style: a soft egg in candy colors that holds a digital creature. It predates the iMac, so it shows the candy blobject already in toys in 1996–97.
The crayon card art is a counter-example to the techno side of Y2K.
borrow: Frame a small pixel display inside a rounded, brightly colored shape.
Use a clear, ribbed plastic bubble as a frame for a product image.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The photograph is © Victoria and Albert Museum, London; the toy and its packaging belong to Bandai.
